title: Dota2 Senate
description: Brute force to optimized: repeatedly rescanning and rebuilding the string versus a two-queue round-robin simulation with a "+n" re-queue offset.

blocks.text: The Dota2 senate consists of senators from two parties: Radiant ('R') and Dire ('D'). Senators act in order (looping back to the start when reaching the end); each senator can either BAN one still-active opposing senator (removing them permanently), or, if all remaining active senators belong to their own party, ANNOUNCE VICTORY. Given a string senate representing each senator's party, predict which party ultimately wins, assuming everyone plays OPTIMALLY (always banning an opponent if possible).

blocks.caption: Two queues of senator indices; whichever senator comes FIRST in the current round always bans the opposing senator who comes next, then re-queues for a future round

blocks.text: Since senators act in their original relative order (looping around), and optimal play always means banning an opponent (never wasting a turn), the entire process can be simulated by tracking each party's ACTIVE senators in a queue, ordered by when they get to act next.

blocks.title: Analogy: Two Teams Taking Turns Eliminating Each Other in Order
blocks.text: Imagine two teams of players, standing in a single combined line in a fixed (repeating) order, where each player, when it's their turn, eliminates the NEXT upcoming player from the OTHER team (since that is always the optimal move: remove a future threat before it can act). Whichever player's turn comes first between the two teams' next available players gets to eliminate the other; the surviving player then gets back in line for a FUTURE turn.

blocks.caption: Two queues (one per party) hold each party's active senators' original positions; the smaller front index always bans the other, then re-queues at position+n for a future round

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Radiant's queue is now empty, so Dire wins, matching the expected result

Before literally simulating each round by scanning and rebuilding the string (potentially many times), notice that tracking each party's ACTIVE senators in a queue (by original index) directly and efficiently models the entire round-robin banning process.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since optimal play always means banning an opponent (there is never a reason to "waste" a turn when an opponent is still active), the process is fully deterministic once positions are known.

Observation 2: Two separate queues, one per party, holding each party's active senators' positions IN ORDER, directly track "who acts next" within each party.

Observation 3: Comparing the FRONT of both queues reveals which party's next senator acts FIRST (the smaller index acts first, since senators act in position order); that senator bans the other party's next senator (the one at the OTHER queue's front).

Observation 4: The SURVIVING senator (the one who just acted) gets to act again in a FUTURE round; re-queuing them at position+n (n = the total senate length) correctly represents "this senator's NEXT turn, one full round later," while preserving the correct relative ordering against senators from the OTHER queue who might also act again later.

Observation 5: The process continues until one queue is completely empty, at which point the OTHER (non-empty) party has eliminated every opponent and wins.
This is a two-queue round-robin simulation: comparing the front indices of both queues determines who acts first and bans the other, with the survivor re-queued at position+n for a future round.

Simulate each round by scanning through the current senate string, having each senator ban the NEXT upcoming opposing senator, building a new (shorter) string each round, repeating until only one party remains.

items: For each round, scan through the current senate string, tracking a "pending ban" for whichever party is due to be banned by the most recently seen senator of the other party.
Build the new senate string for the next round by including only senators who were not banned this round; repeat until only one party remains in the string.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Rebuilding the string each round directly simulates "removing banned senators," correctly reflecting how the senate shrinks over successive rounds.

The "pending ban" tracking correctly handles the WRAP-AROUND nature of banning (a ban decided late in one pass might apply to a senator encountered earlier in the SAME pass, requiring careful bookkeeping).

blocks.text: Correctly simulates optimal play, since it directly tracks which senators survive each round based on who bans whom.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2) in the worst case, since the string can shrink by potentially just one character per full O(n) rescan.
Space: O(n), for the string being rebuilt each round.
Limitation: repeatedly rescanning and rebuilding the string is inefficient; a two-queue simulation directly and efficiently models the SAME round-robin banning process in O(n) total.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rescans the shrinking string every round. Instead, maintain two queues of ORIGINAL indices, one per party. Repeatedly compare both queues' fronts: the smaller index acts first, banning the other party's front senator (which is simply discarded from that queue); the acting senator then re-queues at index+n, representing their NEXT turn one full round later. Continue until one queue empties.

Initialize radiant and dire queues with each party's original indices, in order. While both queues are non-empty: pop both fronts; if the radiant index is smaller, the dire senator is banned (simply not re-queued), and the radiant senator re-queues at index+n; otherwise, the reverse happens. Once one queue empties, the other party has won.
Use two queues of original indices, comparing fronts each round to determine who bans whom, with the survivor re-queued for a future round.

blocks.text: Dire's queue is empty, so Radiant wins, matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n): each senator is added to a queue exactly twice (once for their original position, at most once more for their re-queued position), so the total work is bounded.
Space: O(n), for the two queues.

Since senators act in their ORIGINAL relative order (looping around), the senator with the smaller CURRENT index always acts first. Comparing the two queues' fronts directly identifies this. The optimal move (banning an opponent) is always taken, so the losing senator in each comparison is simply discarded. Re-queuing the survivor at index+n correctly represents them getting another turn exactly one full "round" (n positions) later, correctly maintaining their relative order against future senators from the OTHER party who might also survive and re-queue.

items: The "+n" re-queuing offset is the key trick: it correctly represents "this senator's next turn is one full round later," without needing to explicitly track rounds as a separate concept.

Since a senator is either banned (never re-queued) or survives (re-queued exactly once per round they act in), each original senator contributes a BOUNDED number of total queue operations, keeping the overall algorithm linear.
The final check (which queue is non-empty) directly and simply determines the winning party.

blocks.text: A round-robin elimination process, where participants act in a fixed repeating order and the "winner" of each head-to-head comparison gets another turn later, is a natural fit for TWO queues (one per competing group), comparing fronts and re-queuing survivors at an offset representing "one round later."

items: Forgetting the "+n" offset when re-queuing a surviving senator, which would incorrectly compare their NEXT turn against the WRONG reference point relative to the other party's senators.
Rescanning the string each round (the brute force approach) instead of recognizing the more efficient two-queue technique.
Mishandling the tie case (equal indices), though this specific problem's indices are always guaranteed distinct, since each position holds exactly one senator.

items: Explicitly explaining the "+n re-queue" trick and WHY it correctly represents "one round later" demonstrates a clear understanding of the technique's core insight, not just a memorized pattern.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Two groups alternately eliminate each other in a fixed, repeating turn order" points toward a two-queue simulation, comparing fronts and re-queuing survivors at a "+n" offset.

items: How would you extend this to THREE or more competing parties? A similar multi-queue technique could work, though determining "who acts first" and "who gets banned" among more than two options requires additional tie-breaking logic beyond a simple two-way comparison.

Why is "+n" specifically the correct re-queue offset, rather than some other value? Because there are exactly n total senators (across both parties combined) acting per full round, so adding n to a survivor's current position correctly represents exactly one full round later, keeping their relative order consistent.

How would you determine the EXACT round in which the game ends, not just the winning party? Track the largest re-queued index value reached; dividing it by n (with appropriate rounding) gives the round number in which the game concluded.

A two-queue round-robin simulation, conceptually related to Time Needed to Buy Tickets elsewhere in this category, both involving repeating turn-based processes, though this problem specifically needs BOTH queues compared against each other, rather than a single queue's self-contained simulation.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (two-queue round-robin simulation): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Two-queue round-robin simulation
Core Idea: Two queues (one per party) hold active senators' positions; comparing fronts determines who acts first and bans the other, with the survivor re-queued at position+n for a future round
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)

Most Important Observation: Re-queuing a survivor at position+n correctly represents "their next turn, one full round later," keeping their relative order consistent against the other party's survivors
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Two queues; smaller front index bans the other's front, then re-queues at index+n; last non-empty queue wins
